overview.title: Perception, explained.
overview.metaTitle: Learn about perception and browser experiments | Sense6
overview.description: Research-backed answers about colour vision, response timing, hearing and visual sharpness—and what uncalibrated browser experiments cannot establish.
overview.intro: Explore five questions about what we see, hear and notice. Each explanation connects real research to an interactive Sense6 experiment, with device limits and interpretation boundaries visible.
overview.boundary: Sense6 is a recreational browser lab. These explanations and experiments are not diagnoses, clinical tests or proof of a biological trait.

tetrachromacy-guide.title: Can an online test detect tetrachromacy?
tetrachromacy-guide.metaTitle: Can an online test detect tetrachromacy? | Sense6
tetrachromacy-guide.description: Why RGB screen tests cannot confirm tetrachromacy, what four-cone vision really means, and what colour-discrimination tasks can tell you instead.
tetrachromacy-guide.summary: No ordinary RGB-screen test can demonstrate that you have four functioning dimensions of colour vision. A screen-controlled exercise can describe differences you distinguished on that screen, under those conditions. Establishing functional tetrachromacy is a different research question.

facts.head: The biological question
facts.detail: A fourth type of photopigment does not automatically mean four-dimensional colour perception.

facts.head: The display question
facts.detail: An ordinary screen mixes three primaries. Its output is limited by the display and its calibration.

facts.head: The Sense6 question
facts.detail: Can you discriminate certain colour differences in a short, screen-relative task?

sections.heading: What tetrachromacy actually means
paragraphs: Human colour vision typically begins with three classes of cone photoreceptors whose sensitivities overlap across the visible spectrum. Tetrachromacy concerns a possible fourth independent channel of colour discrimination—not simply being especially observant, naming more shades, or having a large vocabulary for colours.

Genetic variation can create additional cone photopigment classes in some people, especially carriers of certain X-linked colour-vision variants. But the neural visual system must also use that additional signal in a way that changes what a person can distinguish. More photopigments are not, by themselves, proof of a fourth perceptual dimension.

In their 2010 study, Jordan and colleagues tested candidates with several complementary tasks and genetic analyses. Only one of 24 obligate carriers of deuteranomaly showed tetrachromatic behaviour across their tests. This was careful evidence about particular participants and laboratory stimuli, not an internet screening rule.

sections.heading: Why a colourful image on your screen is not a fourth-cone test
paragraphs: Most consumer displays generate visible colours by varying red, green and blue light-producing components. Different numerical RGB values can produce many shades, but the set of stimuli remains constrained by those display primaries, the device gamut, the operating system and the viewer's settings.

To establish an additional perceptual dimension, researchers need spectral stimuli and comparisons designed to separate responses that normally match for three-cone observers. A still image shown through ordinary RGB channels is not an equivalent instrument. Counting bands in a gradient or seeing a hidden number is not evidence of tetrachromacy.

The W3C CSS Color specification describes how browsers represent, convert and display colours within colour spaces. That engineering specification is useful for building reproducible on-screen tasks, but it does not calibrate your screen or reveal the biology of your eyes.

sections.heading: What a browser colour experiment can genuinely explore
paragraphs: A well-described screen task can still be interesting: it can ask you to locate a colour difference, adjust difficulty after responses and record where an abbreviated track happened to finish. These observations depend on the current display, brightness, colour management, ambient light, fatigue and choices made during that run.

Sense6's Screen Colour Lab uses three short observations rather than claiming a single number that ranks colour vision. Its results are deliberately separate, local to the browser and not population thresholds. Repeating under similar lighting and screen conditions may tell you about variation in your own experience; it cannot establish an extra cone class.
If you are curious, try the task as an experiment in what your *screen and setup* let you distinguish. Do not use it to make medical, genetic or diagnostic decisions.

sections.heading: A better question to ask
paragraphs: Instead of “Am I a tetrachromat?”, ask “Which colour differences could I reliably distinguish on this display today, and how did my responses change across a repeated task?” That narrower question has an honest answer within a recreational browser lab.

Further research about functional tetrachromacy would require dedicated stimuli, suitable comparison observers and scientific analysis well beyond an ordinary website. The studies below inform this explanation; none tested or validated the Sense6 implementation.

experiment.hint: Three separate screen-relative observations · about 4 minutes · no tetrachromacy diagnosis

reaction-time-guide.title: How accurate is a reaction-time test in a browser?
reaction-time-guide.metaTitle: How accurate are browser reaction-time tests? | Sense6
reaction-time-guide.description: Understand stimulus display delay, keyboard and touch latency, response timing, medians and why two devices may give different reaction-time readings.
reaction-time-guide.summary: Browser reaction-time results combine human response with display, software and input-device delays. A carefully designed web task can describe a run, but its milliseconds are not an instrument-calibrated measurement of pure human reflex speed.

facts.head: Display
facts.detail: A stimulus can be scheduled before its light reaches your eyes.

facts.head: Response
facts.detail: Keys, touchscreens and operating systems contribute their own latency.

facts.head: Interpretation
facts.detail: Repeated runs on one setup are easier to compare than scores from different devices.

sections.heading: What happens between a signal and the recorded answer?
paragraphs: Imagine a circle changing colour and you pressing a key as soon as you see it. Several stages sit between the instruction to show the colour and the timestamp the page receives: the browser schedules rendering, the display refreshes, you perceive the change, you decide to respond, and the input hardware and operating system deliver an event.

A browser can use a monotonic clock and record events consistently within its own execution model. It still does not have a photodiode measuring the exact moment each pixel lit up or an external instrument measuring when your finger moved. The displayed time reflects the entire chain, including parts outside the page's control.

Touch input and keyboard input can differ. Background tabs, temporary focus loss, power saving, display refresh rate and performance interruptions can introduce additional variation. A result may therefore be useful as an observation without representing a universal biological constant.

sections.heading: What timing research tells us—and what it does not
paragraphs: Bridges and colleagues compared the timing performance of multiple laboratory and online experiment tools using external measurement equipment. Anwyl-Irvine and colleagues likewise tested realistic combinations of online platforms, browsers and devices. Both bodies of work show why timing precision and accuracy depend on implementation and environment.

Those studies do not certify every website that uses browser APIs. In particular, they did not validate the specific stimulus onset, hardware setup or scoring of your current Sense6 session. They support care in reporting timing and checking for interruptions, not the claim that every displayed millisecond equals a calibrated reflex latency.

sections.heading: How to read a reaction-time result
paragraphs: A single fastest response can be influenced by anticipation or chance. In a sequence of responses, a median summarizes the centre of the recorded observations without allowing one unusually slow event to dominate it. False starts, missed signals and interruptions matter too: a neat number can conceal a poor-quality run.

A simple response task and a choice task also ask different things. Reacting when a signal appears is not the same as deciding between left and right responses. Comparing those numbers may be interesting, but it does not isolate one mental process without stronger controls.

Keep both the observed value and its context: input mode, device, screen, interruptions and how much of the scheduled task was completed. If the conditions changed, any apparent improvement may be partly due to hardware rather than practice.

sections.heading: How to make your own comparisons less misleading
paragraphs: Use the same device, input method and similar surroundings when repeating a run. Keep the tab visible, avoid distractions and allow practice to familiarize you with the response. If a run is marked limited or interrupted, treat it as information about that attempt rather than evidence you became slower.

Sense6 records the protocol scope and relevant setup in its local journal so it can distinguish comparable from incompatible runs. It does not upload individual response times or maintain a global leaderboard. Comparing yourself against an invented “average human score” would be much less defensible.
Start with the short Segnale scope if you want to see the mechanics. Its result is a browser-and-device-relative response observation—not a neurological assessment or medical clearance.

color-blindness-guide.title: What can an online colour-blindness test tell you?
color-blindness-guide.metaTitle: What Can an Online Colour Blindness Test Tell You? | Sense6
color-blindness-guide.description: Learn what online colour-vision tasks can reveal, why screen calibration matters, and how they differ from professional colour-vision testing.
color-blindness-guide.summary: An online colour-vision task can show which displayed differences you could distinguish during one run. It cannot, by itself, confirm or rule out a colour-vision deficiency, identify its clinical type, or replace an eye professional's evaluation.

facts.head: A display-relative result
facts.detail: The colours reaching your eyes depend on the screen, software, brightness, filters and surroundings.

facts.head: Different kinds of tasks
facts.detail: Recognising numbers in dot plates, matching lights and finding a gap among dots test related but different abilities.

facts.head: A separate clinical question
facts.detail: Only an appropriately administered and interpreted professional assessment can address diagnosis or a clinical classification.

sections.heading: What is colour-vision deficiency?
paragraphs: Colour-vision deficiency means having difficulty distinguishing some colour differences that many other observers can distinguish. Different types affect different regions or directions of colour perception. It is often inherited, but some acquired eye or health conditions can also affect colour vision.

The phrase “colour blindness” is familiar, but it can be misleading: most affected people still see many colours. A particular screen result cannot establish whether someone has a deficiency or which biological mechanism might explain it. The National Eye Institute recommends talking to an eye doctor if you or your child are concerned about colour vision.

A surprising online result is therefore a reason to ask a better question, not a diagnosis. It may reflect an actual perceptual difference, the device and environment, misunderstanding the instructions or ordinary variation between attempts.

sections.heading: Why online tests and clinical tests are different
paragraphs: Clinicians may use colour plates made of coloured dots, hue-arrangement tasks and—in selected cases—specialist instruments such as an anomaloscope. These are different instruments with different intended interpretations. In a clinical setting, their administration and results can be checked together by a trained professional.

A browser cannot assume that its requested colour values are exactly the colours coming from your screen. Display gamut, colour management, brightness, night-light filters, ambient lighting and visual adaptation can all change the stimulus. Photographs or screenshots of printed colour plates add another uncontrolled transformation.

The National Eye Institute describes professional colour plate, anomaloscope and hue tests. That guidance does not establish that any web page reproducing a similar image has the same diagnostic performance. A result from a consumer screen should not be described as a clinical screening classification.

sections.heading: Why noise, gap choices and control trials matter
paragraphs: Some research instruments deliberately mix colour differences with varying dot brightness so that participants cannot solve the task simply by following an obvious luminance edge. In 1994, Regan, Reffin and Mollon described a computer-controlled colour-discrimination method with luminance noise and masking contours. Their laboratory test helped distinguish patterns of colour sensitivity under controlled conditions.

Daltonia borrows ideas from that family of psychophysical tasks: a C-shaped gap sits inside a field of noisy dots, and three separately sampled display-colour directions adapt during the run. It is not an Ishihara plate, the Cambridge Colour Test, or a certified reproduction of either. A published source about the design principle does not validate the Sense6 task.

The easiest high-contrast presentations serve as task controls: they help show whether you understood and could perform the gap response. Controls and misses affect how cautiously to read the adaptive results. Passing them does not prove normal colour vision; missing them does not diagnose any deficiency.

sections.heading: How to read a Sense6 Daltonia result
paragraphs: Daltonia reports the ending adaptive level of each short, independent on-screen track. Whatever numerical level the task reports, it is not a universal ranking of your eyes: the scale belongs to the stimulus model and current display. A run with few reversals or a boundary reached at the easiest or hardest level is especially limited.

The result also reports high-contrast control responses, bounds and track evidence. Read that context before comparing runs. If you repeat the task, keep the same device, filters, lighting and approximate viewing conditions, and treat any differences as run observations rather than a stable biological trend.

Sense6 stores completed runs locally in your browser's journal, with setup information intended to prevent incompatible comparisons. It does not upload your answers or classify you against a population. If a colour-vision concern affects daily life or an occupational decision, seek an appropriate professional assessment instead of relying on a recreational web result.

hearing-range-guide.title: Can a browser test your hearing range?
hearing-range-guide.metaTitle: Can a browser test your hearing range? | Sense6
hearing-range-guide.description: What online tone tests can reveal, why headphone volume and calibration matter, and why a frequency result cannot diagnose hearing loss or reveal hearing age.
hearing-range-guide.summary: A browser can play tones and record which choices you made on your current headphones and volume setting. It cannot know the sound pressure reaching your ears, so an upper frequency observed online is not an audiogram, a diagnosis of hearing loss, or a measure of 'hearing age'.

facts.head: The digital tone
facts.detail: The browser controls frequency and digital amplitude, not the calibrated sound level at your eardrum.

facts.head: The listening chain
facts.detail: Headphones, fit, volume, room noise and audio processing all affect audibility.

facts.head: The useful result
facts.detail: A run-relative observation that you can revisit under similar conditions, with the limits attached.

sections.heading: A frequency number and a hearing threshold are different
paragraphs: Frequency is the rate of vibration, measured in hertz (Hz). A browser can generate a digital tone at a requested frequency, but hearing that tone also depends on its level and on how that level reaches you. A digital amplitude setting does not tell a website the resulting sound pressure at your eardrum.

Two people may hear different things with the same laptop, and the same person may get a different result when switching headphones or changing volume. Equal numbers on an operating-system volume slider do not guarantee equal acoustic output across devices. An upper frequency noticed on one setup is therefore not a biological upper limit.

A clinical audiogram answers a different question: how sensitive someone is to calibrated sounds at selected frequencies, usually expressed in decibels hearing level (dB HL). That measurement requires known transducers, a suitable test environment and established procedures. The American Speech-Language-Hearing Association's guidelines specify those conditions; Sense6 does not reproduce them.

sections.heading: Why headphones, volume and room noise matter
paragraphs: Every headphone has its own frequency response. Earbuds may fit or seal differently from over-ear headphones; background sounds can mask quiet tones; and the phone or computer may apply equalization, noise reduction or other audio processing. None of these conditions is reliably calibrated by a normal web page.

The Web Audio API defines how the browser creates and processes digital sound. Its audio context reports a sample rate, and frequency generation has mathematical limits related to that rate. The specification does not provide a measurement of your headphone's acoustic output at your ears. At high frequencies, headphone response and playback limits can be especially important.

Turning volume up in search of a higher number is a poor way to learn. Use only a comfortable level, and stop if a sound is uncomfortable. If a task asks you to keep volume unchanged, that instruction protects within-run comparability; it does not make the output clinically calibrated or guarantee that a previous result is comparable on another device.

sections.heading: What Udito actually checks
paragraphs: Sense6's Udito is a recreational listening lab. It begins with headphone-like presentation checks, then asks questions about tones in separate tasks. Its frequency-range observation records where its adaptive sequence ended on this setup. A longer scope also includes pitch-difference choices near selected reference frequencies. Those observations are deliberately not combined into a hearing score.

The task includes known-audibility anchors, control trials and a final check that you did not knowingly change the volume. These make it easier to explain whether a particular run deserves caution. Passing a headphone-like presentation check does not identify the physical device or demonstrate that it is calibrated; failing a check does not diagnose anything either.

When a result reaches the experiment's technical frequency ceiling, that is a limit of what the software attempted, not the highest frequency your ears could possibly hear. If control trials fail, if you are interrupted, or if you change volume, interpret the visible observations cautiously rather than treating them as a reliable personal boundary.

sections.heading: How this differs from a hearing check or audiometry
paragraphs: The World Health Organization's hearWHO app uses digits presented in background noise to provide a hearing check. It has published evidence for that specific task and population, and WHO still says it does not replace professional assessment. A digits-in-noise hearing check and Sense6's browser tone tasks measure different things; validation of the former does not transfer to the latter.

If you have difficulty following conversations or notice a change in hearing, a qualified hearing-care professional can choose the appropriate assessment. An arbitrary online high-frequency result cannot tell you whether you need hearing aids or whether a hearing change is medically significant.

For curiosity, the useful question is narrower: which tone choices could you identify today with this equipment, and were the setup checks coherent? Repeat only under comparable, comfortable conditions, retain the uncertainty and use the private journal as a record of those sessions—not as a clinical hearing history.

visual-acuity-guide.title: Can an online visual-acuity test replace an eye exam?
visual-acuity-guide.metaTitle: Can an online visual-acuity test replace an eye exam? | Sense6
visual-acuity-guide.description: Why screen size, viewing distance and contrast affect online sharpness tasks, and how self-measured acuity observations differ from a professional eye examination.
visual-acuity-guide.summary: No. A screen-based task can describe which small shapes you identified on a particular display at a stated distance. It cannot establish eye health, prescribe lenses, or substitute for a comprehensive examination. Screen calibration and viewing conditions determine how the result should be read.

facts.head: Size on the retina
facts.detail: A target's visual angle depends on its physical size and your distance from the display.

facts.head: Conditions
facts.detail: Screen scaling, viewing distance, contrast, correction and lighting can change your choices.

facts.head: What remains unknown
facts.detail: A sharpness estimate does not examine the retina, eye pressure, visual fields or disease.

sections.heading: Why a target on a screen needs a distance
paragraphs: An eye-chart symbol has a physical size. What matters for recognizing its detail is also the angle it occupies from the viewer's eye. Move closer to the same symbol and its angular size changes, even though its pixels have not. A browser-based sharpness task must therefore connect on-screen size to a viewing distance rather than treating a pixel count as vision.

Pixels reported by a browser are not necessarily physical dots on the panel. Display density, page zoom, operating-system scaling and browser rendering influence how CSS dimensions appear. An on-screen card-size check can help estimate physical scale, while a viewing-distance step helps estimate the resulting visual angle. Both depend on what the participant actually does.

The ISO 8596 visual-acuity standard specifies Landolt-ring optotypes and their presentation for particular distance-vision certification or licensing purposes. It explicitly does not claim to be a standard for clinical measurements. Sense6's self-administered display task is not an ISO-certified acuity test and does not inherit any standard's intended use.

sections.heading: A sharpness result describes a particular task
paragraphs: Many visual-sharpness tasks ask which way a gap faces in a small broken ring. The response depends on the size of that gap, the rendered contrast, the display, focus, attention and the viewing setup. Getting several directions correct says something about those stimuli; it does not reveal a glasses prescription or an eye disease.

A short adaptive sequence can estimate where the person's responses changed during that run. When software reports a model interval, it describes variation under the assumptions of its scoring model. It is not a promise that the screen's scale, the viewing distance or the participant's setup were measured with the same certainty.

A technical display floor or ceiling is another important limit: some gaps cannot become physically smaller on a given screen, and others may exceed the task's chosen range. Results near those boundaries should be labelled as bounded observations rather than presented as exact human visual thresholds.

sections.heading: What Acutezza can record—and what it deliberately cannot
paragraphs: Sense6's Acutezza asks for directional choices on a calibrated-as-possible display setup, with checks for scale and viewing distance. Its Focused scope measures a high-contrast sharpness condition. The longer Standard scope adds a nominal low-contrast condition, which must be interpreted separately. Results are recorded per eye, never as one overall vision grade.

The session remembers whether its scale and distance were measured or assumed, whether task controls were answered coherently, whether the display environment changed, and whether each estimate met a software bound. Those details are part of the result, not technical clutter: without them a small number could appear more certain than it is.

Do not turn an Acutezza result into a '20/20' claim, an astigmatism axis, lens strength, driving eligibility or confirmation of eye health. A weaker or stronger observation may reflect lighting, distance, correction, focus, fatigue or the display just as much as differences in the task.

sections.heading: What a comprehensive examination adds
paragraphs: Visual acuity is only one part of an eye examination. The U.S. National Eye Institute explains that a dilated exam can also check visual fields, eye-muscle function, pupil response and eye pressure, and examine structures such as the retina and optic nerve. A web page that displays letters or gaps cannot perform those assessments.

If your vision changes or you have symptoms, use an eye-care professional rather than relying on a repeated online task. In particular, sudden vision loss, severe pain, new flashes or floaters, or a curtain over the field of view warrant prompt professional assessment. A recreational score should never be used to delay care.

For personal curiosity, repeat the same task only with similar correction, room lighting, screen size and measured distance. Keep left and right eyes separate, note any caution flags, and compare only compatible runs in your private journal. The useful conclusion is about the task you performed—not a diagnosis.
